summary: For ages 5–7, help children recognise and name four well-known dinosaurs — Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and a long-necked giant (Brachiosaurus/Diplodocus) — by anchoring each name to ONE unmistakable visible feature (big head + tiny arms; three horns + frill; back plates + tail spikes; very long neck + small head). This is a naming + single-feature task, kept separate from diet, size or grouping. The aim is picture-cued recall: the child can match name to image unaided and state each one's signature feature, naming from a visible clue rather than guessing.
misconceptions: 'Any big/spiky dinosaur is a T. rex' — T. rex is one specific species with a huge head and tiny arms.
'Stegosaurus and other plated/spiked dinosaurs are the same' — back plates + tail spikes distinguish Stegosaurus.
'Long-necked dinosaurs are pterodactyls/other creatures' — the long-neck giants are sauropods, still dinosaurs.
'All these dinosaurs lived together at the same time' — they lived in different periods (covered later).
'The name describes its diet' — naming and diet are separate; a name like Triceratops means 'three-horned face', not what it ate.

activities.title: Meet the four — name and feature line-up
steps: Look at clear profiles or silhouettes of all four dinosaurs side by side.

For each one, hear its name spoken clearly while pointing to its one stand-out feature: 'Tyrannosaurus rex — huge head and tiny arms', 'Triceratops — three horns and a neck frill', 'Stegosaurus — back plates and tail spikes', 'Brachiosaurus — very long neck and small head'.
Say each name aloud paired with its feature after the adult.
In a later round, answer the lift-the-flap style question for each: 'What makes this one special?' before the feature is revealed again.
activities.insight: Each dinosaur name has a HOOK — a visible feature you can point to — so 'the one with three horns' reliably becomes Triceratops.

activities.title: Match the name to the shape (active recall game)
steps: Drag or place each name label onto the matching dinosaur silhouette.
Try a 'mystery silhouette' round: identify a dinosaur from its outline alone, then name it.
When a match is correct, notice the signature feature being highlighted to confirm.
Say why: 'This is Stegosaurus because of the plates on its back.'
activities.insight: Recognising and naming from shape alone, and justifying with a feature, turns passive recognition into active recall.

activities.title: Which one is it? — check and name from a picture
steps: Answer 'Which one is Stegosaurus?' by choosing from pictures of the four.
Match each name to its described feature (e.g. 'three horns' → Triceratops).

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: shown a big four-legged dinosaur with a very long neck and small head (a shape cue), and a two-legged dinosaur with a huge head, sharp teeth and tiny arms, name each one AND say the feature that helped decide.
activities.insight: Naming rests on a visible feature, not a guess; the 'what feature helped you decide' step blocks pure name-guessing.

checkQuestion: I show you a big four-legged dinosaur with a very long neck reaching up high, and a two-legged dinosaur with a huge head, sharp teeth and tiny little arms. Which is which — name each one — and tell me the feature that helped you decide.
checkAnswer: The long-necked, four-legged one is Brachiosaurus (or Diplodocus) — the long neck for reaching high leaves is the giveaway. The two-legged one with the big head, sharp teeth and tiny arms is Tyrannosaurus rex — the tiny arms and huge toothy head are its signature. Naming rests on a visible feature, not a guess.
